\begin{abstract}
We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, a framework that formally compiles Information Extraction (IE) ontologies into composable token-level decoding constraints via a decidability-guided architecture: a \emph{grammar layer} (context-free) guarantees JSON validity and vocabulary membership; a \emph{semantic layer} (prefix-decidable with state) enforces per-triple domain/range type constraints via a stateful entity registry, with grammar-first fallback when constraints conflict.
Without constraints, Large Language Model (LLM) based IE produces systematic domain/range (DR) violations that persist after fine-tuning, with rates characterized by \emph{constraint tightness} ($\bar{\kappa}$) rather than schema or model scale.
The two layers exhibit a formal enabling dependency (Proposition~1): neither achieves this reduction alone.

66	\section*{Limitations}
67	
68	\paragraph{Constraint scope.}
69	CF impact is model-dependent: for well-calibrated models (Qwen, Llama), S1 introduces CF violations (up to 12.02\%) as a consequence of per-relation independent enforcement; for poorly-calibrated models (Mistral), S1 substantially reduces CF (56.87\%\,$\to$\,1.27\%) by constraining type assignments to schema-valid values.
70	CF fallback ablation shows that eliminating CF re-routes violations to DR ($+$13.85\,pp). CF$\leftrightarrow$DR thus represents a fundamental trade-off in composable constraint systems rather than an independently resolvable limitation (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-dr-tradeoff}).
71	Global entity-level type consensus during decoding offers the most direct path to resolving CF violations.
72	CF type inconsistencies may propagate to downstream tasks that consume extracted triples (e.g., knowledge graph construction, question answering); the impact of such propagation has not been evaluated.
73	Entity F1 impact is model-dependent ($+$1.22\,pp for Qwen vs.\ $-$0.64\,pp for Llama on DocRED), partially confounded by increased parse failures under constraints (Llama: 9.1\% vs.\ 6.8\%).
74	Residual DR under fine-tuning (36 violations across all fine-tuned settings, both models and both datasets) decomposes into entity type errors (39\%), schema coverage gaps (33\%), and model generation errors correctly caught by constraints (28\%); Llama DocRED alone accounts for 33 of 36 residual violations (92\%), reflecting weaker entity typing (Appendix~\ref{app:residual-dr-analysis}).
75	Schema coverage gaps (one-third of residual violations) arise because RE constraints are extracted from training-data type pairs, which may not cover all valid combinations; larger training sets or manual constraint table completion can reduce this gap.
76	
77	\paragraph{Evaluation coverage.}
78	Zero-shot results cover three 7--8B-class models, where relation F1 remains around 4--8\% compared to $\sim$45\% for fine-tuned systems.
79	Zero-shot evaluation covers three 8B-class and one 70B-class model; fine-tuning composability is validated only on 8B-class models.
80	Scaling to smaller models has not been verified, and the dual-factor pattern's predictive scope may differ at other scales.
81	Composability with fine-tuned models is validated on SciERC, DocRED, and WikiEvents with Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B (RE: DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\%, R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp; EE: RoV$\to$0\%, AC$\leq$0.8\%), but evaluation is limited to one fine-tuning method (LoRA); residual CF (Qwen 1.18\%, Llama 0.46\% on SciERC) traces to schema-level type ambiguity (\textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X) rather than enforcement failure.
82	WikiEvents fine-tuning composability is preliminary (20-document test set, the full official split).
83	All main experiments use greedy decoding; our evaluation of beam search on the full SciERC test set (551 documents) and DocRED (50 zero-shot, 998 fine-tuned documents) across three models confirms compatibility (Appendices~\ref{app:sampling},~\ref{app:beam-search}), but comprehensive evaluation across all decoding configurations remains future work.
84	
85	\paragraph{Engineering considerations.}
86	Scalability benchmarks up to 200 entity types and 1,000 relations show constant 2--3\% inference overhead and sub-second compilation ($<$0.5\,s; Appendix~\ref{app:scalability}); however, the first-token uniqueness requirement for continuation masking may become a tokenizer-dependent bottleneck beyond this scale.

\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
\label{sec:discussion}
\input{section7_conclusion_compressed}

% === Limitations (ARR requirement: standalone section, does not count toward page limit) ===
\clearpage
\section*{Limitations}

\paragraph{Constraint scope.}
CF impact is model-dependent: for well-calibrated models (Qwen, Llama), S1 introduces CF violations (up to 12.02\%) as a consequence of per-relation independent enforcement; for poorly-calibrated models (Mistral), S1 substantially reduces CF (56.87\%\,$\to$\,1.27\%) by constraining type assignments to schema-valid values.
CF fallback ablation shows that eliminating CF re-routes violations to DR ($+$13.85\,pp). CF$\leftrightarrow$DR thus represents a fundamental trade-off in composable constraint systems rather than an independently resolvable limitation (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-dr-tradeoff}).
Global entity-level type consensus during decoding offers the most direct path to resolving CF violations.
CF type inconsistencies may propagate to downstream tasks that consume extracted triples (e.g., knowledge graph construction, question answering); the impact of such propagation has not been evaluated.
Entity F1 impact is model-dependent ($+$1.22\,pp for Qwen vs.\ $-$0.64\,pp for Llama on DocRED), partially confounded by increased parse failures under constraints (Llama: 9.1\% vs.\ 6.8\%).
Residual DR under fine-tuning (36 violations across all fine-tuned settings, both models and both datasets) decomposes into entity type errors (39\%), schema coverage gaps (33\%), and model generation errors correctly caught by constraints (28\%); Llama DocRED alone accounts for 33 of 36 residual violations (92\%), reflecting weaker entity typing (Appendix~\ref{app:residual-dr-analysis}).
Schema coverage gaps (one-third of residual violations) arise because RE constraints are extracted from training-data type pairs, which may not cover all valid combinations; larger training sets or manual constraint table completion can reduce this gap.

\paragraph{Evaluation coverage.}
Zero-shot results cover three 7--8B-class models, where relation F1 remains around 4--8\% compared to $\sim$45\% for fine-tuned systems.
Zero-shot evaluation covers three 8B-class and one 70B-class model; fine-tuning composability is validated only on 8B-class models.
Scaling to smaller models has not been verified, and the dual-factor pattern's predictive scope may differ at other scales.
Composability with fine-tuned models is validated on SciERC, DocRED, and WikiEvents with Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B (RE: DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\%, R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp; EE: RoV$\to$0\%, AC$\leq$0.8\%), but evaluation is limited to one fine-tuning method (LoRA); residual CF (Qwen 1.18\%, Llama 0.46\% on SciERC) traces to schema-level type ambiguity (\textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X) rather than enforcement failure.
WikiEvents fine-tuning composability is preliminary (20-document test set, the full official split).
All main experiments use greedy decoding; our evaluation of beam search on the full SciERC test set (551 documents) and DocRED (50 zero-shot, 998 fine-tuned documents) across three models confirms compatibility (Appendices~\ref{app:sampling},~\ref{app:beam-search}), but comprehensive evaluation across all decoding configurations remains future work.

\paragraph{Engineering considerations.}
Scalability benchmarks up to 200 entity types and 1,000 relations show constant 2--3\% inference overhead and sub-second compilation ($<$0.5\,s; Appendix~\ref{app:scalability}); however, the first-token uniqueness requirement for continuation masking may become a tokenizer-dependent bottleneck beyond this scale.
Evaluation covers LoRA and full fine-tuning on 8B-class models; full fine-tuning with an untuned learning rate underperforms LoRA (R-F1 37.89 vs.\ 43.77 on SciERC) but confirms that constraints remain effective across fine-tuning methods (DR 2.74\%\,$\to$\,0\%; Appendix~\ref{app:full-ft}).

1	% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)
2	
3	\section{Introduction}
4	\label{sec:introduction}
5	
6	Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity is guaranteed to carry a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
7	We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
8	Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 1--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates correlate with \emph{constraint tightness} (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
9	Type violations are ontologically invalid regardless of downstream application: a triple whose head or tail type lies outside the relation's domain/range specification contradicts the schema definition.
10	At deployment-grade quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption; reliable type-safety enforcement is needed.
11	
12	Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
13	Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
14	Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} guarantees syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
15	Post-hoc filtering improves precision but discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives, sacrificing recall; at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it becomes impractical.
16	Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime guarantees.
17	These two directions—grammar-constrained decoding and schema-aware training—have developed independently; no method provides both semantic awareness and runtime enforcement.
18	
19	We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that formally compiles IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
20	A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} enforces context-free constraints (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} enforces prefix-decidable constraints (pair-based domain/range) through dynamic logit masking over a runtime entity registry, with an \emph{enabling dependency} between layers.
21	OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from any IE ontology, requires no constraint-specific training, and applies to any autoregressive LM.
22	We evaluate two deployment configurations: LoRA + greedy S1 eliminates DR with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp and $+$10\% latency; LoRA + beam S1 ($k{=}4$) additionally resolves the CF trade-off, achieving zero violations on SciERC (1.54$\times$ latency).
23	Zero-shot evaluation across four models (8B--70B) confirms DR drops by 76--99\% for calibrated models.
24	
25	Our contributions:
26	\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
27	    \item A formal ontology-to-constraint compilation framework: we classify IE type constraints by decidability (context-free, prefix-decidable with state, non-local), yielding a two-layer architecture with pair-based sequential enforcement and formal guarantees at each level (\S\ref{sec:decidability}). % Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity is guaranteed to carry a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 1--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates correlate with \emph{constraint tightness} (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
Type violations are ontologically invalid regardless of downstream application: a triple whose head or tail type lies outside the relation's domain/range specification contradicts the schema definition.
At deployment-grade quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption; reliable type-safety enforcement is needed.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} guarantees syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering improves precision but discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives, sacrificing recall; at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it becomes impractical.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime guarantees.
These two directions—grammar-constrained decoding and schema-aware training—have developed independently; no method provides both semantic awareness and runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that formally compiles IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} enforces context-free constraints (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} enforces prefix-decidable constraints (pair-based domain/range) through dynamic logit masking over a runtime entity registry, with an \emph{enabling dependency} between layers.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from any IE ontology, requires no constraint-specific training, and applies to any autoregressive LM.
We evaluate two deployment configurations: LoRA + greedy S1 eliminates DR with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp and $+$10\% latency; LoRA + beam S1 ($k{=}4$) additionally resolves the CF trade-off, achieving zero violations on SciERC (1.54$\times$ latency).
Zero-shot evaluation across four models (8B--70B) confirms DR drops by 76--99\% for calibrated models.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item A formal ontology-to-constraint compilation framework: we classify IE type constraints by decidability (context-free, prefix-decidable with state, non-local), yielding a two-layer architecture with pair-based sequential enforcement and formal guarantees at each level (\S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from any IE ontology.
    \item An analytical framework linking constraint tightness to enforcement outcomes: $\bar{\kappa}$ characterizes dataset-level DR reduction (94--99\% at $\bar{\kappa}{<}0.5$ vs.\ 42--90\% at $\bar{\kappa}{>}0.8$), with entity type confusability as the critical co-factor; $\bar{\kappa}$ additionally determines post-hoc resolution feasibility (Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).
    \item Empirical validation of the enabling dependency and composability: the five-way ablation confirms that neither layer alone achieves $>$24\% DR reduction, while their composition yields 94--100\%; fine-tuning does not obviate constraints (residual DR 1--2\% at R-F1 40--46\%); the framework generalizes to event extraction with 245 constraints across three tokenizer families (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
\end{enumerate}

The mean tightness $\bar{\kappa} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r} \kappa(r)$ characterizes schema restrictiveness.
Tighter constraints eliminate more grammar-valid tokens at type-bearing positions; fallback frequency and residual DR increase accordingly.
This dual-factor pattern (tightness $\times$ baseline violation rate; $n{=}4$ model--dataset pairs, descriptive) aligns with the cross-dataset results: SciERC ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$) achieves 94--99\% DR reduction vs.\ DocRED ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$) at 45--90\%; the full range across three models is 42--99\% (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}; Appendix~\ref{app:dual-factor}).
The pattern extends to WikiEvents EE ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.82$; Appendix~\ref{app:wikievents-kappa}).
However, $\kappa$ is necessary but not sufficient for high violation rates: per-relation analysis shows that high-$\kappa$ relations with unambiguous entity types (\textsc{place\_of\_birth}, $\kappa{=}0.92$, DR${=}$0\%) have zero violations, while relations with comparable $\kappa$ but confusable types (\textsc{basin\_country}, $\kappa{=}0.97$, DR${=}$74.6\%) are highly vulnerable (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa-case-study}).
$\bar{\kappa}$ provides deployment guidance: schemas with $\bar{\kappa} < 0.5$ achieve near-complete DR elimination under zero-shot S1 (94--99\% reduction); schemas with $\bar{\kappa} > 0.8$ require fine-tuning to narrow the fallback regime (DR\,0.01--0.21\%).
$\bar{\kappa}$ also determines post-hoc resolution feasibility: low-$\bar{\kappa}$ schemas ($<$0.5) benefit from TCR with negligible DR regression ($\leq$0.28\,pp), while high-$\bar{\kappa}$ schemas ($>$0.8) suffer harmful DR increases (up to $+$9.38\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).

\paragraph{Non-Rectangularity and Sequential Masking.}
\label{sec:rectangularity}
% Data source: artifacts/rebuttal/w2_rectangularity_report.md
Sequential masking is necessary because ontology type signatures are non-rectangular (0/7 SciERC, 23/96 DocRED relations satisfy $\sigma(r) = \operatorname{dom}(r) \times \operatorname{range}(r)$); independent enforcement would admit 33--37\% spurious pairs.

\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
Fine-tuning narrows the fallback regime: DR drops to $\leq$\,0.21\% and CF to $\leq$\,1.18\%, with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp; the grammar layer becomes a no-op and the semantic layer alone reduces residual DR by 39--72\% (\S\ref{sec:composability}).

\begin{abstract}
We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, a framework that formally compiles Information Extraction (IE) ontologies into composable token-level decoding constraints via a decidability-guided architecture: a \emph{grammar layer} (context-free) guarantees JSON validity and vocabulary membership; a \emph{semantic layer} (prefix-decidable with state) enforces per-triple domain/range type constraints via a stateful entity registry, with grammar-first fallback when constraints conflict.
Without constraints, Large Language Model (LLM) based IE produces systematic domain/range (DR) violations that persist after fine-tuning, with rates characterized by \emph{constraint tightness} ($\bar{\kappa}$) rather than schema or model scale.
The two layers exhibit a formal enabling dependency (Proposition~1): neither achieves this reduction alone.
% exp_ids: w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval
Composed with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), \textsc{OntoCoDec} eliminates DR violations with negligible R-F1 impact ($\pm$0.6\,pp); beam search ($k{=}4$) resolves the cross-field consistency (CF) trade-off, achieving zero violations on SciERC (R-F1 44--46, 1.54$\times$ latency).
Under zero-shot decoding, DR drops by 76--99\% for calibrated models.
The framework extends to event extraction without modification, validating the ontology-agnostic compilation design.
\textsc{OntoCoDec} compiles constraints automatically from any IE ontology at inference time, requires no constraint-specific training, and applies to any autoregressive LM across four models (8B--70B) and three tokenizer families.
\end{abstract}

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity is guaranteed to carry a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 1--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates correlate with \emph{constraint tightness} (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
Type violations are ontologically invalid regardless of downstream application: a triple whose head or tail type lies outside the relation's domain/range specification contradicts the schema definition.
At deployment-grade quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption; reliable type-safety enforcement is needed.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} guarantees syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering improves precision but discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives, sacrificing recall; at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it becomes impractical.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime guarantees.
These two directions—grammar-constrained decoding and schema-aware training—have developed independently; no method provides both semantic awareness and runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that formally compiles IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} enforces context-free constraints (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} enforces prefix-decidable constraints (pair-based domain/range) through dynamic logit masking over a runtime entity registry, with an \emph{enabling dependency} between layers.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from any IE ontology, requires no constraint-specific training, and applies to any autoregressive LM.
We evaluate two deployment configurations: LoRA + greedy S1 eliminates DR with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp and $+$10\% latency; LoRA + beam S1 ($k{=}4$) additionally resolves the CF trade-off, achieving zero violations on SciERC (1.54$\times$ latency).
Zero-shot evaluation across four models (8B--70B) confirms DR drops by 76--99\% for calibrated models.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item A formal ontology-to-constraint compilation framework: we classify IE type constraints by decidability (context-free, prefix-decidable with state, non-local), yielding a two-layer architecture with pair-based sequential enforcement and formal guarantees at each level (\S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from any IE ontology.
    \item An analytical framework linking constraint tightness to enforcement outcomes: $\bar{\kappa}$ characterizes dataset-level DR reduction (94--99\% at $\bar{\kappa}{<}0.5$ vs.\ 42--90\% at $\bar{\kappa}{>}0.8$), with entity type confusability as the critical co-factor; $\bar{\kappa}$ additionally determines post-hoc resolution feasibility (Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).
    \item Empirical validation of the enabling dependency and composability: the five-way ablation confirms that neither layer alone achieves $>$24\% DR reduction, while their composition yields 94--100\%; fine-tuning does not obviate constraints (residual DR 1--2\% at R-F1 40--46\%); the framework generalizes to event extraction with 245 constraints across three tokenizer families (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 1--2\% but leaves residual violations that vary by schema tightness (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
On SciERC ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$), adding S1 eliminates or near-eliminates DR: Qwen 1.95\%\,$\to$\,0\%, Llama 1.11\%\,$\to$\,0.09\%, with R-F1 within $\pm$0.1\,pp.
On DocRED ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$, 96 relations), S1 reduces DR from 0.76\% to 0.01\% (Qwen, $\downarrow$99\%) and 0.49\% to 0.21\% (Llama, $\downarrow$57\%); R-F1 changes are $-$0.30\,pp and $+$0.06\,pp.
The lower Llama-DocRED reduction (57\% vs.\ 92--100\%) traces to higher tightness ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$), which triggers grammar-first fallback more frequently.
Across all four model-dataset settings, DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp.

LoRA + greedy S1 is the recommended fast deployment configuration: DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\%, CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\% at R-F1 40--46, with $+$10\% latency overhead (\S\ref{sec:runtime}).
Beam search ($k{=}4$) with LoRA eliminates all four violation types on SciERC for both Qwen and Llama (R-F1 44.23, 46.11; \S\ref{sec:beam-results}).

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity is guaranteed to carry a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 1--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates correlate with \emph{constraint tightness} (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
Type violations are ontologically invalid regardless of downstream application: a triple whose head or tail type lies outside the relation's domain/range specification contradicts the schema definition.
At deployment-grade quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption; reliable type-safety enforcement is needed.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} guarantees syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering improves precision but discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives, sacrificing recall; at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it becomes impractical.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime guarantees.
These two directions—grammar-constrained decoding and schema-aware training—have developed independently; no method provides both semantic awareness and runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that formally compiles IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} enforces context-free constraints (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} enforces prefix-decidable constraints (pair-based domain/range) through dynamic logit masking over a runtime entity registry, with an \emph{enabling dependency} between layers.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from any IE ontology, requires no constraint-specific training, and applies to any autoregressive LM.
We evaluate two deployment configurations: LoRA + greedy S1 eliminates DR with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp and $+$10\% latency; LoRA + beam S1 ($k{=}4$) additionally resolves the CF trade-off, achieving zero violations on SciERC (1.54$\times$ latency).
Zero-shot evaluation across four models (8B--70B) confirms DR drops by 76--99\% for calibrated models.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item A formal ontology-to-constraint compilation framework: we classify IE type constraints by decidability (context-free, prefix-decidable with state, non-local), yielding a two-layer architecture with pair-based sequential enforcement and formal guarantees at each level (\S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from any IE ontology.
    \item An analytical framework linking constraint tightness to enforcement outcomes: $\bar{\kappa}$ characterizes dataset-level DR reduction (94--99\% at $\bar{\kappa}{<}0.5$ vs.\ 42--90\% at $\bar{\kappa}{>}0.8$), with entity type confusability as the critical co-factor; $\bar{\kappa}$ additionally determines post-hoc resolution feasibility (Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).
    \item Empirical validation of the enabling dependency and composability: the five-way ablation confirms that neither layer alone achieves $>$24\% DR reduction, while their composition yields 94--100\%; fine-tuning does not obviate constraints (residual DR 1--2\% at R-F1 40--46\%); the framework generalizes to event extraction with 245 constraints across three tokenizer families (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
\end{enumerate}
